title: Growth arrest of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in acidic environments enhances their survival of antibiotic treatment
experiments_summary:
1. FDAA labeling (fixed-cell imaging): Six Mtb strains (CDC1551, H37Rv, four clinical isolates) were adapted to pH 7.0, 6.2, or 5.9 for 1–4 days. Nascent peptidoglycan was labeled with fluorescent D-amino acid RADA (25 µM, 6 h) to identify growing versus nongrowing cells. Heat-killed cells served as negative controls. Fixed cells were imaged on a widefield DeltaVision microscope; segmentation was performed with ilastik and CellProfiler pipelines. Additional controls assessed viability after regrowth, effect of starting OD, and pH-dependence across three pH levels.

2. Time-lapse pulse-chase live-cell imaging: CDC1551 cells pre-labeled with HADA were loaded into custom PDMS microfluidic devices under continuous neutral or acidic media flow. Cells were imaged every hour for 120 h. Growth dynamics were tracked by measuring pole extension of HADA-negative (new) growth regions. Cells were manually annotated using ObjectJ and classified as growing, nongrowing, or converting to nongrowing using MATLAB-based smoothing and linear regression criteria.

3. Null model simulation: Simulated instantaneous single-cell growth rate datasets were generated under a uniform-slowing null model, parameterized to match population-averaged growth rates of experimental neutral and acidic conditions. Simulated and experimental growth rate distributions were compared using 20-h rolling window smoothing.

4. Antibiotic dose-response assay (resazurin): Mtb strains were adapted to pH 7.0 or pH 5.9 for 4 days, then treated with ethambutol, isoniazid, rifampicin, or linezolid across a concentration range for 10 days in 384-well plates. After drug removal via transfer onto charcoal agar (to sequester antibiotics), cells recovered for 10 days. Bacterial survival was measured by resazurin fluorescence (Ex. 530 nm, Em. 590 nm). HADA-labeled versus unlabeled cultures were compared to confirm HADA did not affect ethambutol susceptibility.

5. Live-cell ethambutol tolerance imaging: CDC1551 cells were adapted to pH 5.9 for 4 days and labeled with HADA during the final 12 h. Cells were loaded into microfluidic devices and treated with 245 µg/ml ethambutol for 2 days using conditioned media, followed by 8 days recovery in drug-free unbuffered media. Regrowth of HADA-positive (previously growing) versus HADA-negative (nongrowing) cells was tracked by time-lapse imaging and manually annotated.

6. PhoPR mutant fixed-cell imaging: CDC1551 WT, ΔphoPR, and phoPR-complemented (phoPR*) strains were adapted to pH 7.0, 5.9, or 5.7 for 4 days and labeled with HADA (25 µM, 6 h). Cells were imaged on a Zeiss Axio Observer 7 microscope. Polar HADA labeling patterns were compared across strains to assess PhoPR's role in nongrowing cell formation. FM 4-64 membrane permeability staining was also performed to assess whether phoPR deletion altered membrane properties.

7. CFU-based ethambutol survival assay: CDC1551 WT, ΔphoPR, and phoPR* strains were adapted to pH 7.0 or pH 5.9, then treated with 8 or 24 µg/ml ethambutol for 10 days. After washing, cells were serially diluted and plated on 7H10 agar; colonies were counted after 3 weeks. Biological triplicates were used.

8. RNA sequencing: Biological triplicates of CDC1551, and two clinical isolates (V1, V3) were adapted to pH 7.0 or pH 5.9 for 1 or 4 days. RNA was extracted using bead-beating in triazol and RNeasy cleanup with on-column DNase digestion. Ribodepleted paired-end sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Reads were aligned to the M. tuberculosis Erdman reference genome using Geneious Prime; differential expression was determined with DESeq2 (p < 0.05). Genes differentially expressed in the same direction across all three strains were subjected to pathway and gene regulator enrichment analysis using Fisher's exact test with a curated annotation file.
